paragraphs: The core deliverable of natural sciences managers is turning a research direction into executable projects: setting objectives and budgets, organizing people and equipment resources, advancing research progress, and ensuring data and compliance requirements, rather than doing only administrative work.

Complete one small exercise using public materials: write the objectives, milestones, budget items, role assignments, and risk contingency plan for a virtual research project, and then ask someone with management experience to give feedback against project review standards.

Positive signals: willing to make priority trade-offs amid uncertain research results, responsible for others' work results, and able to explain decision bases with data and records; caution signals: avoiding conflict and performance conversations, unable to carry budget and compliance responsibility, or willing to do only personal research and not to coordinate others.

Paper exercises and public materials practice do not constitute performance authorization, budget approval authority, or employment management authority; when personnel, financial, and safety compliance judgments are involved, authorized personnel must act per employer systems and local regulations.

entries: Set research directions, stage objectives, and annual plans and allocate resources.
Compile and execute project budgets, and monitor funding and equipment use.
Organize and coordinate research projects, and schedule progress and delivery milestones.
Recruit, train, guide, and evaluate the performance of researchers and technicians.
Establish and enforce data, experimental record, and safety compliance requirements.
Review research results and reports, and decide whether to advance or adjust the direction.
Represent the team in communication with funders, partner institutions, or regulators.
Promote cross-department collaboration and results translation, and handle conflicts and resource competition.

paragraphs: Natural sciences managers ({{fact:identity}}) plan, direct, or coordinate activities and research and development work in fields such as life sciences, physical sciences, mathematics, and statistics: setting objectives and budgets, organizing research projects, managing personnel and compliance requirements, and being responsible for the team's research results and external commitments.

Work context (O*NET work context survey, United States respondent percentages): 100% use email daily, 88% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 84% hold face-to-face discussions daily, and 42% use the telephone daily; 56% work more than 40 hours per week and 90% have a regular work schedule; 52% say they can decide tasks and priorities themselves with a great deal of freedom; 71% consider precision or high accuracy extremely important; 32% consider the consequences of error extremely serious; 40% carry very high responsibility for the health and safety of others and 56% carry very high responsibility for the work results of others.

The daily loop is usually: set the direction and objectives → allocate people and budget → advance projects and monitor progress → review data and compliance → adjust the direction and communicate externally → review the team and resources. Management decisions need to leave a traceable basis.

O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone 5 (SVP 8.0 and above), with most positions requiring graduate education and many requiring 5 years or more of related experience; the interest code is {{fact:interest-code}}, indicating that the work involves research judgment, organizational coordination, and standardized management.

The difference from adjacent positions lies in the scope of responsibility and the object: research scientists focus on specific topics and experimental conclusions, project managers focus on schedule and delivery, and this occupation is also responsible for people, budgets, compliance, and the team's long-term research direction.

Software or tools mentioned in job postings (such as statistical software and project management and office software) only indicate the management environment and technology preferences; they do not prove that all positions require these tools, nor that automation has been achieved.

Capability evidence for management positions comes from reviewable records: project plans and budget execution, review and decision bases, team development and performance records, and the handling of compliance and safety incidents.

The biggest difference between natural sciences managers and adjacent occupations is the scope of responsibility: this occupation is responsible for direction, people, budgets, and compliance, research scientists are responsible for topic conclusions, and project managers are responsible for schedule and delivery.

The comparison basis is each occupation's official task descriptions and employer responsibility statements; the same job title may correspond to different task combinations in different organizations, and this page only makes directional distinctions and does not represent mutual recognition of qualifications.

The table below compares this occupation with adjacent directions by main object, core output, and authorization boundary, to help judge which real tasks to look at rather than choosing by title similarity.

It takes the overall arrangement of research direction, people, and budget as its core object and delivers executable projects and compliance records; research scientists deliver the experimental design and conclusions of specific topics as their core output.

If you would rather make direction trade-offs, develop people, and coordinate resources, compare this occupation; if you would rather invest long term in a single topic and experimental data analysis, compare research scientists.

Students and career changers: first complete one project planning exercise using public materials, confirm whether you are willing to carry budget, personnel, and compliance responsibility, and only then discuss tool speed-up.
Use tools for materials retrieval, progress organizing, and drafting reports; personnel evaluation, funding approval, and compliance judgments must be done by people with the responsibility.
Project and research managers: tools may help organize project data and risk lists, while direction trade-offs and resource allocation remain your responsibility.
Do not submit undisclosed research data, participant information, or partner materials to unauthorized services; conclusions must be checked back against original records and project files.
Department heads: tools may help with scenario analysis of staffing and budgets, while performance conclusions and personnel decisions are still confirmed by authorized personnel.
Responsibility does not change because of tools: data security, research integrity, funding compliance, and personnel management responsibility remain with managers and institutions.

Institutions and compliance leads: specify which tools may be used, the scope of data that may be processed, and the record-keeping requirements, and state the situations that must be reported or approved.

Read employment evidence separately: the O*NET wages and employment use the exact 11-9121.00 occupation scope, and the page has not published generative AI adoption rates or job change data for this occupation, so they cannot be pieced together into a replacement conclusion.

Insufficient evidence: no national occupational wage median under the same scope as O*NET 11-9121.00 was obtained this round; the National Bureau of Statistics industry annual averages can serve as a reference for related research and development service employers but are not equal to income in this occupation.
In 2025, the average annual wage of employed persons in scientific research and technical services in urban non-private units in mainland China was {{fact:cn-wage-nonprivate}}.

In 2025, the average annual wage of employed persons in scientific research and technical services in urban private units in mainland China was {{fact:cn-wage-private}}; non-private and private are two different statistical scopes, cannot be mixed, and exclude self-employed individuals and freelancers.

Actual pay for this occupation also depends on the city, the type of institution (universities, research institutes, state-owned enterprises, or foreign research and development centers), team size, funding sources, and the performance structure, and should be verified against public job postings and contracts.
The wage shown on the United States O*NET page is {{fact:us-wage}}, a median, not starting pay or a personal quote.
This wage statistic cannot be interpreted as starting pay, a personal quote, or an income promise; percentiles are only statistical positions and do not represent experience or job level.
When comparing United States positions, also verify the state, industry (professional and technical services, government), institution size, funding cycles, and benefits structure.
The O*NET page does not mark a parent occupation or combined scope, so this page presents it under the exact occupation scope and does not mix it with adjacent management occupations.
A job offer should be verified against employer recruitment information and local rules; official statistics only describe the employed population they cover.
United States figures cannot be directly converted into or extrapolated as individual income in mainland China.
